summary: Specifies how RADIUS operates over IPv6 and defines the RADIUS attributes used for IPv6 network access.

eli5.summary: It teaches the guard who checks logins to work with the new, longer addresses.

questions: which radius attribute numbers are used for ipv6
subtitle: Six new RADIUS attributes that let network access servers hand out IPv6 addresses, prefixes and routes.

tldr.problem: RADIUS could authenticate users and configure their access, but it had no attributes to carry IPv6 addresses, interface identifiers, prefixes or routes.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines six attributes, numbered 95 to 100, covering the NAS address, interface identifier, prefix, login host, route and prefix pool. It also says RADIUS may run over IPv4 or IPv6 transport.
tldr.outcome: A RADIUS server can now tell a NAS which IPv6 settings a user gets. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 8044.

today: RFC 3162 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 8044. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This RFC specifies the operation of RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial In User Service) over IPv6, as well as the RADIUS attributes used to support IPv6 network access.

A NAS (network access server) sending an Access-Request may not know in advance whether the host will use IPv4, IPv6 or both. In PPP, for example, IPv6CP happens after LCP, so address assignment does not occur until RADIUS authentication and authorization are complete. The IPv6 attributes may therefore be sent along with IPv4 attributes in the same message, and the NAS decides which to use. The NAS SHOULD only allocate addresses and prefixes the client can actually use.

The NAS can provide IPv6 access natively, or through IPv6-within-IPv4 tunnels or 6over4. That choice has no effect on RADIUS itself, though tunnel attributes should be used if a tunnel to a particular location is wanted.
sections.eli5: The guard at the door does not know yet which kind of address a visitor will use, so the guard can be given notes for both kinds and picks the right one.

sections.title: Identifying the NAS, the Interface and the Prefix
sections.content:
NAS-IPv6-Address (type 95, length 18) carries the 16-octet IPv6 address that identifies the NAS requesting authentication. It SHOULD be unique to the NAS within the scope of the RADIUS server and appears only in Access-Request packets. NAS-IPv6-Address and/or NAS-IP-Address MAY be present; if neither is, NAS-Identifier MUST be.

Framed-Interface-Id (type 96, length 10) carries an 8-octet IPv6 interface identifier for the user. It MAY be used in Access-Accept packets. If the Interface-Identifier IPv6CP option has been negotiated, the attribute MUST be included in the Access-Request as a hint. Servers are recommended, but not required, to honor it.

Framed-IPv6-Prefix (type 97) indicates an IPv6 prefix, and the matching route, to configure for the user. It MAY appear in Access-Accept packets and can appear several times. In an Access-Request it is a hint the server need not honor. Since the NAS is assumed to set up the route for the prefix, the server does not need to also send a Framed-IPv6-Route for it.

Its Length is at least 4 and no larger than 20. The Reserved octet MUST be present and is always zero. Prefix-Length is 0 to 128 bits, and the Prefix is up to 16 octets, with bits outside the Prefix-Length zero.
sections.eli5: These notes say who the door guard is, which house number to give the visitor, and which whole street of house numbers they may use.

sections.title: Login Host, Routes and Prefix Pools
sections.content:
Login-IPv6-Host (type 98, length 18) names the system to connect the user to when the Login-Service attribute is included. Its 16-octet address has special values: all ones (0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF) means the NAS SHOULD let the user choose an address or name, and 0 means the NAS SHOULD pick a host. Any other value is the address the NAS SHOULD connect the user to.

Framed-IPv6-Route (type 99, length at least 3) gives routing information to configure for the user on the NAS, in Access-Accept packets, possibly several times. The text SHOULD hold a destination prefix, optionally a slash and decimal length, a gateway address, and one or more decimal metrics, all separated by spaces. When the gateway is the unspecified address, the user's IP address SHOULD be used as the gateway.

Framed-IPv6-Pool (type 100, length at least 3) names a prefix pool configured on the NAS that SHOULD be used to assign the user's prefix. A NAS that does not support multiple prefix pools MUST ignore it.
sections.eli5: More notes say which computer to send a visitor to, which roads lead to their house, and which neighborhood of addresses to pick from.

sections.title: Which Attributes Go in Which Packets
sections.content: The RFC's table lists how many of each attribute may appear in each packet kind. For example, NAS-IPv6-Address may appear 0 or 1 times in an Access-Request or Accounting-Request and never in an Access-Accept. Framed-IPv6-Route and Framed-IPv6-Pool never appear in a request. Framed-IPv6-Route may appear several times in an Access-Accept, and Framed-IPv6-Pool at most once. None of the six may appear in Access-Reject or Access-Challenge packets.
sections.eli5: A chart shows which note may go in which kind of envelope and how many copies you may put in.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
In IPv6-enabled networks RADIUS may run over IPv4 or IPv6. Known RADIUS vulnerabilities are described in the cited RADIUS documents. Because IPsec is mandatory to implement for IPv6, the RFC expects IPv6-capable RADIUS implementations will typically run over IPsec.

RADIUS uses its shared secret to hide attributes such as User-Password, to compute the Response Authenticator and for the Message-Authenticator, so the secret gives confidentiality, integrity and authentication. Only IPsec ESP with a non-null transform can substitute for that application-layer security. With AH or ESP null, a RADIUS shared secret will typically still be needed. With ESP and a non-null transform, the secret MAY NOT be configured, and then a shared secret of zero length MUST be assumed.
sections.eli5: The guard and the office share a secret password to prove messages are real. If the messages travel in a locked, secure tube, they may not need the password.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The RFC needs six new RADIUS attribute numbers, for NAS-IPv6-Address, Framed-Interface-Id, Framed-IPv6-Prefix, Login-IPv6-Host, Framed-IPv6-Route and Framed-IPv6-Pool. The registered numbers are 95 to 100, as listed in the table of attributes.
sections.eli5: Each new note needs its own number in the official list, so the six notes got numbers 95 to 100.

items.label: NAS-IPv6-Address
items.desc: IPv6 address identifying the NAS; Access-Request only.

items.label: Framed-Interface-Id
items.desc: IPv6 interface identifier for the user.

items.label: Framed-IPv6-Prefix
items.desc: IPv6 prefix and route for the user.

items.label: Login-IPv6-Host
items.desc: Host to connect the user to.

items.label: Framed-IPv6-Route
items.desc: Routing information to configure on the NAS.

items.label: Framed-IPv6-Pool
items.desc: Name of the prefix pool to assign from.
